## **Euclid's Core Mathematical Method: Sphere Circumscription**

Euclid's primary mathematical approach for establishing regularity was remarkably elegant: for each Platonic solid, he:

<title>Dice</title>
<fragment>
Dice are often sold in sets, matching in color, of six different shapes. Five of the dice are shaped like the Platonic solids, whose faces are regular polygons. Aside from the cube, the other four Platonic solids have 4, 8, 12, and 20 faces, allowing for those number ranges to be generated. The only other common non-cubical die is the 10-sided die, a pentagonal trapezohedron die, whose faces are ten kites, each with two different edge lengths, three different angles, and two different kinds of vertices. Such sets frequently include a second 10-sided die either of contrasting color or numbered by tens, allowing the pair of 10-sided dice to be combined to generate numbers between 1 and 100.


Using these dice in various ways, games can closely approximate a variety of probability distributions. For instance, 10-sided dice can be rolled in pairs to produce a uniform distribution of random percentages, and summing the values of multiple dice will produce approximations to normal distributions.[29]

![](image)The Zocchihedron is approximately 1.5 inches (38 mm) in diameter.
**Zocchihedron** is the trademark of a 100-sided die invented by Lou Zocchi, which debuted in 1985. Unlike other polyhedral dice, it takes the appearance of a ball with 100 flattened spots. It is sometimes called "Zocchi's Golfball".


Zocchihedra are designed to provide percentage rolls in games, particularly in role-playing games.




## History

[edit]

It took three years for Zocchi to design his die, and three more years to get it into production. Since its introduction, Zocchi has improved the design of the Zocchihedron, filling it with teardrop-shaped free-falling weights to make it settle more swiftly when rolled.


The Zocchihedron II is a further improved model, and has another filler.



## Probability distribution of rolls

[edit]

A test published in *White Dwarf* magazine concluded that the frequency distribution of the Zocchihedron was substantially uneven. Jason Mills noticed that some numbers were spaced closer together than others, and suspected that this non-uniform placement would cause some numbers to predictably come up more than others. Mills performed 5,164 rolls and the results confirmed these suspicions; some numbers came up significantly more than others. Most notably, rolls of more than 93 or less than 8 were significantly rarer than middling results. Not coincidentally, these numbers were all spaced closer together near the "poles" of the die, as opposed to numbers near the "equator" that are more widely spaced.[1]


After the test was published, the numbering on the Zocchihedron was redesigned with higher and lower numbers placed more evenly across all parts of the die. While numbers spaced closely together near the "poles" still come up less often, the numbers that are placed in these areas are more evenly distributed between 1 and 100, instead of consisting mainly of very high and very low numbers.



## Patents

[edit]

The aesthetic appearance of the Zocchihedron was protected by United States design patent D303,553,[2] which expired on 19 September 2003. The original patent did not include mention of any internal braking mechanism.[3] There was never a utility patent for the original Zocchihedron, although United States patent 6,926,276[4] may protect the braking mechanism of the Zocchihedron II. That patent will expire on 9 August 2025 and applies only to "spherical dice" containing "multi sized and irregularly shaped particles".

- **Geometric shape:** Octahedron  
- **Platonic solid:** **True**
- **Why it qualifies:** All 8 faces are regular equilateral triangles, and 4 faces meet at each vertex. It resembles two square pyramids attached base-to-base.

### 4. **D10 (10-sided)**
- **Geometric shape:** Pentagonal trapezohedron
- **Platonic solid:** **False**
- **Why it doesn't qualify:** The faces are **kites** (four-sided polygons with unequal edges and angles), not regular polygons. It has two different types of vertices: sharp corners where 5 faces meet, and blunter corners where 3 faces meet.

### 5. **D12 (12-sided)**
- **Geometric shape:** Dodecahedron
- **Platonic solid:** **True** 
- **Why it qualifies:** All 12 faces are regular pentagons, and 3 faces meet at each vertex.

### 6. **D20 (20-sided)**

- **Platonic solid:** **True**
- **Why it qualifies:** All 20 faces are regular equilateral triangles, and 5 faces meet at each vertex.

- **Geometric shape:** Zocchihedron (spherical with flattened spots)
- **Platonic solid:** **False**
- **Why it doesn't qualify:** It's not even a true polyhedron - it takes the appearance of a ball with 100 flattened spots rather than having flat faces that are regular polygons arranged symmetrically.

### **D10 (Pentagonal Trapezohedron):**
- **Irregular faces:** Uses kite-shaped faces instead of regular polygons
- **Unequal vertex arrangements:** Has two different vertex types (3-face and 5-face meeting points)
- **Lacks symmetry:** The mix of different vertex types breaks the perfect symmetry required for Platonic solids

### **D100 (Zocchihedron):**
- **Not a polyhedron:** It's essentially a sphere with flattened spots
- **Irregular geometry:** The 100 "faces" are not regular polygons and don't follow the mathematical rules of polyhedra
- **Practical compromise:** Designed for gaming convenience rather than geometric perfection

## Summary

**Only 5 of the common gaming dice are Platonic solids: D4, D6, D8, D12, and D20.** The D10 and D100 exist as practical gaming solutions but don't meet the strict geometric requirements for Platonic solids, which demand regular polygon faces and identical vertex configurations throughout the shape.

This explains why role-playing games commonly use 5 dice that are mathematically perfect (the Platonic solids) plus the D10 as a practical addition for generating percentage rolls, even though it breaks the perfect geometric pattern.
